### Consonants

| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Nasal** | m |  |  | n |  |  |  |  |  |  |
| **Plosive** | p · b |  |  | t · d |  | c |  | k · ɡ |  | ʔ |
| **Affricate** |  |  |  |  | dʒ |  |  |  |  |  |
| **Sibilant fricative** |  |  | s̪ | s | ʃ |  |  |  |  |  |
| **Non-sibilant fricative** |  | f · v | ð |  |  |  |  |  | ʁ | h |

Where symbols share a cell, the voiceless ones come first and the voiced follow the dot. Secondary articulation (ʷ ʲ ˠ ˤ) and length (ː) stay in the cell of the plain sound.

### Vowels

| | Front | Back |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Close** | i iː ḭ | u uː ṵ |
| **Open-mid** |  | ɔː |
| **Near-open** | æ æː | ɔ̞ ɔ̞ː |
| **Open** | a aː a̰ |  |

Unrounded vowels come before the dot, rounded after it. Length: long vowels iː æː ɔː uː ɔ̞ː aː. Nasality: no nasal vowels. Phonation: ḭ ṵ a̰.

### Tone, syllables and stress

No phonemic tone.
Syllable shapes (share of syllables in the word-shape model): CV 33%, CVC 29%, CCV 13%, CCVC 10%, V 4%, VC 3%. At most 2 consonant(s) before the vowel and 1 after it.
Stress falls on the first syllable. The IPA on this page marks it with ˈ before the stressed syllable.
Core words average 1.47 syllables (3.2 sounds); 31% of words share their form with another word.

### Allophony

This output records no allophones (the engine stores sounds as phonemes only).

### Phonological rules

Rules the language applies today, in order. A new sound change starts as a rule applying across words; as it ages it narrows to words, then to word-making, and in the end dies, leaving its alternations in single words.

| # | rule | applies | since | example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | l → r / C_ | only where words are made (derivation, compounds, new words, loans) | ~9 kyr ago | us̪ + læ → us̪ræ 'arm or hand + nose (compound)' |
| 2 | j → ∅ / V_V | only where words are made (derivation, compounds, new words, loans) | ~3 kyr ago | nḭj + -ɔ̞ː → nḭɔ̞ː 'day (not night)-do' |
| 3 | ∅ → b / m_r, m_l | inside words: affixes and compounds | ~2.5 kyr ago | nim + læ → nimblæ 'be alive + nose (compound)' |
| 4 | n → ŋ / _# | inside words: affixes and compounds | ~2 kyr ago | – |
| 5 | a → ∅, aː → ∅, a̰ → ∅, i → ∅ / C_s#, C_r#, C_n#, C_l# (final-syllable syncope before a final sonorant or s) | inside words: affixes and compounds | ~2 kyr ago | i- + næːl → inl 'agent-where' |
| 6 | s → h / #_, V_V | inside words: affixes and compounds | ~1 kyr ago | – |
| 7 | ʔ → ∅ / #_ (loss of the initial glottal stop) | inside words: affixes and compounds | ~1 kyr ago | – |
| 8 | f → h / #_, V_V | inside words: affixes and compounds | ~1 kyr ago | nuf + -ɔ̞ː → nuhɔ̞ː 'egg-do' |

Lately dead: S239 (crowded out by younger rules, 0.5 kyr ago); S004 (crowded out by younger rules, 0.5 kyr ago); S050 (crowded out by younger rules, 0.5 kyr ago); S102 (crowded out by younger rules, 0 kyr ago); S076 (crowded out by younger rules, 0 kyr ago); S008 (crowded out by younger rules, 0 kyr ago).

## Orthography

The house romanization in two registers: the full spelling (workbench, one letter or digraph per sound, tone marks) and the book spelling (lossy: no tone, plain vowels, and at most 2 diacritic letters kept for the whole language; one spelling per sound in every word). Allophones are spelled as their phonemes.

**Consonants:** m ‹m› · n ‹n› · p ‹p› · b ‹b› · t ‹t› · d ‹d› · c ‹ky› · k ‹k› · ɡ ‹g› · ʔ ‹'› · dʒ ‹j› · s̪ ‹s̮› ‹s› · s ‹s› · ʃ ‹sh› · f ‹f› · v ‹v› · ð ‹dh› · ʁ ‹ġ› · h ‹h› · j ‹y› · w ‹w› · l ‹l› · r̃ ‹rr›

**Vowels:** i ‹i› · ḭ ‹ḭ› ‹i› · iː ‹ii› · u ‹u› · ṵ ‹ṵ› ‹u› · uː ‹uu› · ɔː ‹oo› · æ ‹æ› ‹ae› · æː ‹ææ› ‹aee› · ɔ̞ ‹o̱› · ɔ̞ː ‹o̱o̱› · a ‹a› · a̰ ‹a̰› ‹a› · aː ‹aa›

Where two spellings are given the second is the book spelling.

## Grammar

Basic word order is SVO; it has prepositions. In the noun phrase: possessor before the possessed; noun before the adjective; noun before the demonstrative; numeral before the noun; noun before the relative clause. Overall it is head-initial.
It has a definite article after the noun, no indefinite article, no case marking on nouns, no alignment marking (subject and object are not told apart by form), singular and plural, no gender or noun classes.
Verbs mark progressive and habitual; there is an indirect (reported or inferred) evidential. Negation uses a negator before the verb; yes/no questions use a final question particle. Verbs agree with the subject by prefixes and with the object by suffixes.
Other features: numeral classifiers; serial verbs; verb reduplication; a copula; a periphrastic causative; a bound passive; question words moved to the front; a decimal counting base; a 'have' verb for possession.
Measured morphology: 22 live grammatical markers, mean bondedness 1.6 (0 free word … 3 fused), 60 paradigm cells, 29 of them with allomorphy.

### Grammar sketch

Built from the typology and the live markers above (planet/language/sentences.py); where the engine tracks no marker for a construction, the form is the word such markers commonly grow from, and the text says so. Examples are glossed by the Leipzig rules (abbreviations under Sample sentences).

**Number.** Nouns mark number: plural: a prefix (iː, from 'all').

| *iː* |
| --- |
| dog |

‘dog’

| *iː-jiː* |
| --- |
| PL-dog |

‘dogs’

**Case.** Nouns have no case marking. Subject and object are not marked apart: word order tells them. Place and company are said with the plain words 'in' (æːh), 'at' (hɔːm), 'with' (im) as adpositions.

**Gender and noun classes.** Nouns are counted with classifiers (free words, not yet bound to the noun): class 1 for a single person, and for every noun no other class takes, a separate word after the numeral (iːf, from 'person').

| *if* | *iːf* | *iː-kiː* |
| --- | --- | --- |
| two | CLF | PL-man |

‘two men’

**Tense and aspect.** Verbs mark tense and aspect. Progressive (PROG): a separate word before the verb (aj, from 'walk'); habitual (HAB): a prefix (h; hæː in some words (sound change at the join); from 'know'). Unmarked: past, future, perfective (left to context).

| *aj* | *hah* |
| --- | --- |
| PROG | go |

‘(it) is going’

| *hæː-hah* |
| --- |
| HAB-go |

‘(it) usually goes’

**Mood and evidentiality.** Speakers mark how they know: reported (evidential) (REP): a separate word before the verb phrase (maj, from 'say'). Mood markers: hortative ('let us') (HORT): a prefix (hiː, from 'come').

| *maj* | *hah* |
| --- | --- |
| REP | go |

‘(it) goes, they say’

| *hiː-hah* |
| --- |
| HORT-go |

‘let us go’

**Person agreement.** Verbs agree with the subject: 1SG: a clitic before the verb (hu, from 'I'); 3SG: a prefix (hiː, from 'he'); 1PL: a prefix (kuː, from 'person'); 2PL: a clitic before the verb (nuː, from 'you'); 3PL: a prefix that fuses with some stems (æː, from 'they'). No marker yet for 2SG (zero).

| *hu=hah* |
| --- |
| 1SG=go |

‘I go’

| *hiː-hah* |
| --- |
| 3SG-go |

‘he/she goes’

| *kuː-hah* |
| --- |
| 1PL-go |

‘we go’

**Object agreement.** Verbs also agree with the object: 2PL.OBJ: a clitic after the verb (ɔːʃij, from 'you'). No marker yet for 1SG.OBJ, 2SG.OBJ, 3SG.OBJ, 1PL.OBJ, 3PL.OBJ.

| *hiː-hiːj=ɔːʃij* |
| --- |
| 3SG-see=2PL.OBJ |

‘he/she sees you all’

**Negation.** Negation is a prefix (biː, from 'nothing').

| *hu* | *hu=biː-jiːjih* | *ubu-ɡ* |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1SG | 1SG=NEG-drink | milk-DEF |

‘I do not drink the milk.’ (sentence 6 below)

**Questions.** Yes/no questions use a particle at the end of the clause. Question words move to the front: who hiːf, what lɔ̞ː, where næːl, when naw, how haw.

| *kuːdʒtim* | *hi* | *mɔːmac-ɡ* | *lɔː* |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |

‘Do you hear the thunder?’ (sentence 4 below)

| *lɔ̞ː* | *mipla-ɡ* | *hiː-jiḭ* |
| --- | --- | --- |
| what | child-DEF | 3SG-bring |

‘What does the child bring?’ (sentence 5 below)

**Commands.** There is no imperative marker: a command is the bare verb stem, with no subject and no subject or tense marker. 'Let us ...' has a hortative marker of its own.

| *hiː* | *kammɔːf-ɡ* |
| --- | --- |
| eat | fish-DEF |

‘Eat the fish!’ (sentence 12 below)

| *kuː-hiː-hiː* | *kammɔːf-ɡ* |
| --- | --- |
| 1PL-HORT-eat | fish-DEF |

‘Let us eat the fish!’ (sentence 16 below)

**Possession.** The possessor stands before the possessed noun, with no marker. 'Having' is said with a 'have' verb ('my mother has a boat').

| *kiː-ɡ* | *iː* |
| --- | --- |
| man-DEF | dog |

‘the man's dog’

| *hu* | *ʃbi* | *hiː-jiːb* | *mɔːʔaw* |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1SG | mother | 3SG-have | boat |

‘My mother has a boat.’ (sentence 7 below)

**Relative clauses.** Relative clause after the noun, introduced by the word for 'that' (as English that and German der grew from a pointing word).

| *ʃbi-ɡ* | *ɡbiːnaf* | *hiː-nuːr̃a* |
| --- | --- | --- |
| woman-DEF | REL | 3SG-dance |

‘the woman who dances’

**Copula.** The copula is a separate word before the verb phrase (ɡbiːnaf, from 'that').

| *kiː* | *ɡbiːnaf* | *ɡbiːnaf* | *iːlaj* |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| man | that | COP | merchant |

‘That man is a merchant.’ (sentence 9 below)

| *ub-ɡ* | *ɡbiːnaf* | *hibbuhɔ̞ː* |
| --- | --- | --- |
| water-DEF | COP | cold |

‘the water is cold’

**Voice.** The passive is a prefix (kuː, from 'get'): the object of the active verb becomes its subject and the doer is left out.

| *kammɔːf-ɡ* | *hiː-kuː-hiːj* |
| --- | --- |
| fish-DEF | 3SG-PASS-see |

‘The fish is seen.’ (sentence 13 below)

**Reduplication.** Verbs reduplicate for an action done again and again, or by many (ITER), by copying the stem's first consonant and vowel before it.

| *ha-hah* |
| --- |
| ITER-go |

‘(an action done again and again, or by many)’

| *kiː-ɡ* | *hiː-bɔ̞-bɔ̞* | *kammɔːf-ɡ* |
| --- | --- | --- |
| man-DEF | 3SG-ITER-hit | fish-DEF |

‘The man hits the fish again and again.’ (sentence 15 below)

**Serial verbs.** Verbs can be strung together in one clause with one subject (serial verbs): 'take X come' is 'bring'. 'Go' after a motion verb gives its direction ('run go' = run away).

| *kiː-ɡ* | *hiː-juː* | *kammɔːf-ɡ* | *hub* |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| man-DEF | 3SG-take | fish-DEF | come |

‘The man brings the fish (takes it and comes).’ (sentence 14 below)

| *ɔːɔ̞ː* | *hah* |
| --- | --- |
| run | go |

‘run away’

**Giving (two objects).** No dative: a serial construction, 'take the thing, give (it to) the person'.

| *ʃbi-ɡ* | *hiː-juː* | *kammɔːf-ɡ* | *iːvṵf* | *mipla-ɡ* |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| woman-DEF | 3SG-take | fish-DEF | give | child-DEF |

‘The woman gives the child a fish.’ (sentence 11 below)

**Numerals.** Counting is decimal: numbers above ten are built from ten and the units. Twenty is muːif and a hundred is cṵb.

| *iæ* |
| --- |
| 11 |

‘11 = 10 + 1 ('ten' and 'one')’

| *huːd* |
| --- |
| 15 |

‘15 = 10 + 5 ('ten' and 'five')’

| *æh* |
| --- |
| 30 |

‘30 = 10 × 3 ('ten' and 'three')’

**Valence.** The verb changes how many participants it takes: reciprocal (RECP): a prefix (hɔː, from 'other').

| *iː-kiː-ɡ* | *æː-hɔː-hiːj* |
| --- | --- |
| PL-man-DEF | 3PL-RECP-see |

‘The men see each other.’ (sentence 18 below)

**Linking clauses.** Complement clauses stand bare, with no complementizer.

| *kiː-ɡ* | *hiː-maj* | *iː-ɡ* | *hiː-kumʃij* |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| man-DEF | 3SG-say | dog-DEF | 3SG-sleep |

‘The man says that the dog sleeps.’ (sentence 17 below)

**Word shapes.** HAB and 1PL together are one ending, kuːh, that does not split into the two (cumulative exponence); some markers sound the same: 3SG and HORT are both hiː; 1PL and PASS are both kuː (context tells them apart).

| *kuːh-hah* |
| --- |
| HAB.1PL-go |

‘we usually go’

**Demonstratives.** Demonstratives count two distances: 'this' ɡbi (near) and 'that' ɡbiːnaf (far).

| *iː* | *ɡbi* |
| --- | --- |
| dog | this |

‘this dog’

| *iː* | *ɡbiːnaf* |
| --- | --- |
| dog | that |

‘that dog’

**Comparison.** An 'exceed' comparison: 'A is big, exceeds B', with the verb for 'climb' (as Yoruba ju 'exceed', Thai kwaa 'cross over').

| *kiː-ɡ* | *ɡbiːnaf* | *dʒis̪* | *hḭc* | *iː-ɡ* |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| man-DEF | COP | big | exceed | dog-DEF |

## Names of people and places

**Naming tradition.** Given names are one meaningful word; the byname is the father's name in the genitive with 'son' or 'daughter'. The tradition goes back to the hobgoblin proto-language.

| **Mooġih** | /mɔːʁih/ | 'gift' | old | Mooġih 'gift': mooġih 'gift'; an old name, coined in d159 4.0 kyr ago as Mookhw |
| **Bu** | /bu/ | 'tall' | new | Bu 'tall': bu 'tall'; coined from today's words |
| **Mayġuw** | /majʁuw/ | 'spring' | new | Mayġuw 'spring': mayġuw 'spring'; coined from today's words |
| **Inġii** | /inʁiː/ | 'wolf' | new | Inġii 'wolf': inġii 'wolf'; coined from today's words |
| **Iib Yahkiihae** | /iːb jahkiːhæ/ | 'bear, son of strong' | patronymic | the father's name Hae + yahkii 'son' (compounded: the language has no genitive marker) |
| **Hae Aemooġih** | /hæ æmɔːʁih/ | 'strong, daughter of gift' | patronymic | the father's name Mooġih + ae 'daughter' (compounded: the language has no genitive marker) |

**Settlements.** **Livuvihu** /livuvihu/ (village, 1,239): 'the old fence'; named by the human (d561.1) who founded it 2.1 kyr ago, kept as heard; **Naali** /naːli/ (village, 1,210): 'Huyufuba's field'; village + the old name: 'village Huyufuba's field' (a tautology, like River Avon); named by the human (d561.1) who founded it 2.6 kyr ago, kept as heard; **Nayhuvrru** /najhuvr̃u/ (village, 1,133): 'the big village'; village + the old name: 'village big village' (a tautology, like River Avon); named by the human (d561.1) who founded it 2.2 kyr ago, kept as heard.

## Texts

Each sentence in four lines: the book spelling, the IPA with its morph breaks, the gloss, and the English.

### A fable: The Bird and the Fish

One fixed short fable, told in every language as August Schleicher told his in Proto-Indo-European (1868), so that the same text shows what sound change and grammar change did. English: A bird sat in a tree. The bird saw a fish in the water. The bird said: “Come! I will give you a good seed.” The fish said: “I do not eat seeds. You will eat me.” The fish did not come. The bird ate the seed.
